summary: A 1970 paper on systems for interprocess communication in a resource-sharing computer network, by D. C. Walden. It replaces RFC 61 and looks at how programs on separate computers can communicate.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 62 proposes a way for programs in one time-sharing system, and later across network sites, to exchange messages. It describes the design as a proposal and reports that it had not been implemented.

subtitle: A 1970 proposal for message exchange between processes on networked computers.

tldr.problem: A resource-sharing network needs processes on different computers to communicate in a systematic way.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal defines monitor operations such as SEND and RECEIVE using numbered ports, then generalizes matching across sites with a distributed Network Controller.
tldr.outcome: The author says the system was not implemented and that the paper is not an official BBN position.

facts.label: Monitor operations
facts.value: SEND, RECEIVE, RECEIVE ANY, SEND FROM ANY, SLEEP, UNIQUE

today: The metadata lists RFC 62 as Unknown, and the document says it supersedes RFC 61. The author describes it as an unimplemented proposal, not an official BBN position.

sections.title: Interprocess Communication
sections.content:
D. C. Walden frames resource sharing as a problem of communication between processes, because resources are associated with processes. The paper first describes operations for processes in one time-sharing system and then generalizes them to remote processes.

The author states that this is not an official BBN position on Host protocol for the ARPA Computer Network.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal treats communication between programs as the key to sharing computer resources. It begins with programs on one computer and then considers programs at different sites.

sections.title: SEND, RECEIVE, and Ports
sections.content:
The monitor provides SEND, RECEIVE, RECEIVE ANY, SEND FROM ANY, SLEEP, and UNIQUE operations. SEND and RECEIVE identify a send port, receive port, message buffer, and restart location.

A port is a data path identified by a unique number. The monitor matches a SEND and RECEIVE with the corresponding port numbers and transfers the message. A SEND waits until a matching RECEIVE occurs; unmatched operations can time out, while RECEIVE ANY does not time out.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender and receiver use matching port numbers to arrange a message. The system starts transferring data only when the receiver has issued a matching RECEIVE.

sections.title: Communication Across Sites
sections.content:
For remote processes, a Network Controller performs the SEND and RECEIVE matching. It can sit at the center of a star network or have its functions distributed across sites.

A rendezvous site keeps a table of unmatched requests. A RECEIVE identifies that site, where a matching SEND can meet it; the message then travels to the site that issued the RECEIVE. The RFC also discusses ways to allocate unique numbers and move ports between sites.
sections.plainLanguage: For remote processes, a designated site matches the sender's and receiver's requests. Once they match, the message is delivered to the receiving site's process.

sections.title: ARPA Network Example and Limits
sections.content:
The paper discusses applying the design to the ARPA Network and suggests placing the communication operations in the IMPs. It describes the network at the time as ten sites connected through IMPs and 50-kilobit phone lines.

Walden states that the proposed system had not been implemented, so he had no performance reports. His conclusions are explicitly described as subjective claims.
sections.plainLanguage: The author suggests a role for IMPs in carrying out these operations on the ARPA Network. He also says the proposal had not been built or measured.
